prize_parts.citation: For developing empirical methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets, which made structural analysis of industries possible.

statement.case_for: The Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes framework, with Berry (1994) as its identification precursor, solved a concrete problem: how to estimate substitution patterns and markups when prices are endogenous and products are differentiated. It is a single, well-bounded methodological discovery with unusually clear credit. Pakes' dynamic-industry work extends it into entry, investment and merger analysis. Three decades of use in merger review, antitrust, auctions, trade, health and environmental economics show that it has been tested in practice, not just cited. The field has no recent recognition. I weigh this on discovery, attribution and maturity, not on how many colleagues rank it. The test I would apply is the one I care about in my own field: a method that turns theory into estimates on real data and has demonstrably changed practice and policy.
statement.case_against: Structural IO results rest on functional-form and equilibrium assumptions, and estimated markups and merger predictions can be sensitive to them. The three-name limit also leaves out Bresnahan and Reiss, whose empirical-IO tradition predates BLP, and Benkard and Levin, who worked on dynamic games. The committee could judge that a prize for BLP alone understates the field's breadth. Pakes' share is arguably larger than the other two names', which makes the attribution less symmetrical than it looks.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B006 first and proposes only Kiyotaki and Moore. He argues that Gertler and Gilchrist build on Bernanke-Gertler, that Bernanke's 2022 prize already covers part of the accelerator, and that the two-person attribution is cleanest.
responses.response: I agree with the two-name attribution, which is why I proposed Kiyotaki and Moore alone. I also agree the work is mature and was tested by 2007-09. Where I differ is on the weight of the 2022 overlap. Even with a clean attribution, it makes B006 less of a new step than a field with no recent recognition. I rank Kiyotaki-Moore as a strong alternative and would not oppose it, but I do not think the 2022 overlap is settled. I also note that Hassler's own uncertainties say the empirical identification of the collateral channel is mixed. That is a weaker evidentiary base than BLP's decades of applied use.

responses.point: Andersson puts B047 first with Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes. He notes that the methods are used routinely in merger review, auctions and regulation, and that the field has no recent recognition. He concedes that the three-name cap leaves out Bresnahan, Reiss, Levin and Benkard.
responses.response: I share this reading, including the attribution. The BLP trio is the cleanest credit allocation in the pool. I would qualify one point: I do not think the exclusion of Bresnahan is costless. The committee should say openly that the citation recognises the demand-estimation and dynamic-industry methods, not the whole empirical-IO tradition. That is why my citation is worded narrowly. I would not widen the group at the cost of a diffuse credit.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B006 first. He argues that collateral constraints and the financial accelerator became the standard way macro models handle credit frictions, and that the 2008 crisis vindicated them. He also ranks B047 second, with the same trio I propose.
responses.response: I accept that B006 is a foundational mechanism and that the 2008 vindication matters. I disagree that Gertler belongs with Kiyotaki and Moore on this prize. Krusell himself concedes that the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist lineage overlaps with prior recognition and that this is a defensible but not unique split. That makes the B006 trio less clean than the BLP trio. If the committee prefers macro-finance, I would back the two-name version. Krusell's own second-place ranking of B047, with the same trio, suggests we agree on the attribution.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B023 first with Autor, Hanson and Katz. He treats the task-based framework and the import-shock evidence as one body of work that is conceptually clear, widely replicated and policy-relevant.
responses.response: I rank B023 third and agree it is credible and influential. My reservation is attribution, which is where I differ from Fredriksson. The China-shock papers belong to Autor, Dorn and Hanson, while the task and skill-bias work involves Katz and others outside the credited names. Fredriksson himself notes the choice of three is a judgement call. A bundle that merges two discoveries and leaves out Dorn is harder to defend than a single method with a clear core. I therefore rank it behind B047 even though I find the scientific contribution substantial.

uncertainties: How the committee weighs a methodological and applied-econometric contribution against foundational theory such as B006.
Whether the citation should reach the Bresnahan-Reiss empirical-IO tradition or the dynamic-games contributors, which the three-name cap excludes.
How much weight to give the 2022 overlap for B006 and the Krugman overlap for B036, since colleagues draw different conclusions from the same facts.
I rely on background knowledge of the literature and have not independently verified citation or usage data.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for the proposed laureates Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes. The profile lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to them. My general affiliations (SSE, Swedish House of Finance, adjunct at Chicago Booth, KVA Vice President) are noted for transparency, and the profile does not show any specific connection to a shortlisted candidate. My corporate-finance field is distant from structural IO.
